analysis.one_liner: Limits how many patents biologic drugmakers can assert in lawsuits against cheaper biosimilar competitors.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee approved the bill in a November 2019 markup, but it was never formally reported to the House or voted on before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company wants to sell a cheaper copy of an expensive biologic drug, the original maker can sue it for patent infringement — sometimes stacking up dozens or even a hundred patents, one for each tweak in the drug or its manufacturing. This bill would cap how many patents the original maker can use in such a lawsuit: 20 total, with no more than 10 of the kind filed more than four years after the drug was approved. Courts could lift the cap for good cause, and the cap would not apply to patents on how the drug is used medically.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and payers who buy expensive biologics, such as drugs for arthritis, cancer, and diabetes. Faster biosimilar competition typically brings steep price cuts — brand-name makers have used large numbers of patents to keep cheaper versions off the market for years.

how_it_helps.text: Caps at 20 the number of patents a biologic maker can assert in a lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant, with no more than 10 issued after the drug was approved [S2][S3].

Targets patents filed more than four years after market approval and manufacturing-process patents not actually used by the original maker — the late-added patents commonly used to stretch a monopoly [S2][S3].
Lets a court raise the limit if the interest of justice or good cause requires it, so the cap has a safety valve [S2][S3].
Applies only when the biosimilar maker completes the required information-sharing steps with the original maker, preserving the existing negotiation process [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic manufacturers, whose patent thicket litigation is a primary tool for extending market exclusivity and premium pricing after their core patents expire.

drawbacks.text: The cap is not absolute: a court can increase the number of patents for good cause, and the limit never applies to patents claiming methods of using the drug, leaving a major patent-stacking avenue open [S2][S3].
Weaker patent enforcement in biosimilar litigation could reduce expected returns on follow-on biotech research, which is the standard objection from the research-based drug industry.

The bill addresses only one barrier to biosimilar entry; FDA exclusivity periods, regulatory complexity, and rebating practices would still shape whether cheaper versions actually reach patients or how much prices fall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is narrow but real: patent thickets are a documented way brand biologic makers delay cheaper competition for years, and a litigation cap directly targets that tactic. The carve-out for method-of-use patents and the court's good-cause escape valve soften the bill, and price relief depends on biosimilars actually launching afterward. Still, the costs fall on a concentrated industry while the gains accrue broadly to patients and payers.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee voted in a markup to send the bill to the floor, but the committee never formally reported it out and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 25, 2019 by Rep. Hank Johnson with Rep. Martha Roby as original cosponsor, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S3][S4][S5].

Referred to the Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet Subcommittee on August 28, 2019; that subcommittee discharged it on November 19, and the full committee held a markup on November 21, ordering the bill reported as amended [S5].
Despite clearing the markup step, the bill was never formally reported to the House and never received a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers keep their ability to assert unlimited numbers of patents in biosimilar lawsuits, preserving the litigation strategy that keeps cheaper competitors tied up in court for years.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and advocated for it through the House Judiciary Committee markup.

for.name: Rep. Martha Roby
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's original Republican cosponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Allowed the committee to order the bill reported in a November 2019 markup but never formally reported it out or scheduled it for a House floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill and one Republican cosponsored it, but no floor vote was ever taken, so the broader partisan split was never recorded.

industries.note: These makers use large patent portfolios — sometimes dozens to more than a hundred patents on a single drug — to delay biosimilar competition for years after core patents expire, keeping prices high for patients. The bill caps how many patents they can assert in a single lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant.

With fewer patents asserted per lawsuit, litigation becomes shorter and cheaper, letting these firms bring lower-priced versions to market sooner. Their gain is patients' gain, since biosimilars typically sell at substantial discounts.

The bill leaves method-of-use patents fully enforceable and lets courts raise the cap for good cause, so core biotech exclusivity remains intact; the main effect is on late-filed patents used to extend monopolies at the margin.
